item.title: Create a collection
item.description:
Create a collection #

Creates a new collection.

Examples #

The following request creates a new collection called my-collection in the namespace my-namespace:

PUT /my-namespace:my-collection

If creating a collection within the default namespace, it can be simplified as:

PUT /my-collection

Request # 

PUT /[<namespace>:]<name>

Path parameters #

  • <namespace>
    (Optional, string) The namespace which the collection belongs to. Namespace names must meet the following criteria:
    • Lowercase only
    • Cannot include \ /, *, ?, ", <, >, |, , ,, #
    • Cannot start with -, _, +
    • Cannot be . or ..
    • Cannot be longer than 255 bytes (note it is bytes, so multi-byte characters will count towards the 255 limit faster)
  • <name>
    (Required, string) Name of the collection you wish to create. Collection names must meet the same criteria as namespace names.

Query parameters #

  • <wait_for_active_shards> \

item.title: Delete a collection
item.description:
Delete a collection #

Delete an existing collection.

Examples #

The following request deletes the collection called my-collection:

DELETE my-collection

Request # 

DELETE /[<namespace>:]<name>

Path Parameters #

  • <namespace>
    (Optional, string) The namespace which the collection belongs to.
  • <name>
    (Required, string) Name of the collection you wish to delete.

item.title: Update collection schema
item.description:
Update collection schema #

Apply an additive schema diff (new or updated field definitions) to an existing collection. The change is replicated through Raft and every shard engine of the collection picks it up.

Field deletion is not supported by design — a schema diff can only add or update properties.

item.title: Update collection settings
item.description:
Update collection settings #

Update the collection-level settings of an existing collection. The change is applied through the Raft-replicated metadata request, so it survives restarts and reaches every node.

Examples #

Change the default replica count used for newly allocated rollings:

PUT /my-collection/_settings
{
 "rolling": { "number_of_replicas": 2 }
}

Restrict the collection’s shard copies to two nodes:

PUT /my-collection/_settings
{
 "routing": {
 "allocation": {
 "include": { "_id": "node-a,node-b" }
 }
 }
}

item.title: Compact a collection
item.description:
Compact a collection #

Queue one manual compaction (merge) pass on every started primary copy of the collection, cluster-wide. Useful when you want to reclaim disk space or reduce the segment count on demand, without waiting for the background compaction cadence.

The API is asynchronous: it fans out to at most one request per node hosting a started primary, and each node queues its own batch compaction job (one job per node, mutual exclusion — HTTP 409 from that node’s row while one runs). The request returns as soon as the jobs are queued; a pass can run for minutes, so nothing waits for the merges. Per-shard job state and live merge progress (phase, per-mille) are observable in each node’s task view, and a job is cancellable there too. A node-level failure fails that node’s row, not the whole request.

item.title: Flush a collection
item.description:
Flush a collection #

Queue a flush of every live shard copy of the collection, cluster-wide — primaries and started replicas. A flush seals the shard’s mutable state into the WAL and builds a new immutable .fire segment from the WAL tail, turning in-memory writes into durable segment storage so the WAL can be purged afterwards.

Both a flush and a Compact a collection request queue node-local jobs that run asynchronously — the request returns as soon as the jobs are queued. Track or cancel them on the node’s task list (GET /_node/_local/tasks): flush jobs under flush_jobs, compaction under compaction_tasks[]. Only one flush job runs per node at a time — a node already running one answers 409 in its row. The difference is what the job does: compaction merges existing immutable segments, a flush seals the mutable tail into a new one.

item.title: Roll over a collection
item.description:
Roll over a collection #

Allocate a new rolling for the collection now, regardless of whether the active rolling is full — subsequent writes go to the new rolling. This is the manual form of the automatic rollover that happens when a rolling reaches its document capacity.

The change is replicated through Raft (the same metadata request used by automatic rollovers), so the shard groups of the new rolling are created on every node.

item.title: Update rolling settings
item.description:
Update rolling settings #

Adjust the replica count of an existing rolling: every shard group of the rolling gains new unassigned replica shards (allocated by the shard allocator when capacity allows) or has its extra replicas removed, and the rolling’s number_of_replicas setting is updated.

This is the leaf-most level of the layered settings model — it overrides the collection-level default for this rolling only.

item.title: Reshard a rolling
item.description:
Reshard a rolling #

Change the number of shards of a rolling, online. Splitting raises the shard count (finer partition ranges, e.g. 1 → 2); merging lowers it (e.g. 2 → 1).

The reshard builds a hidden target rolling while the source keeps serving every read and write. Existing documents are streamed into the target with their _id preserved, the write tail is replayed until the target converges, and a single metadata commit then swaps the target in atomically. Documents stay addressable under the same _id and _key throughout, including for writes issued while the reshard is building.

item.title: Salting (salt-split routing)
item.description:
Salting (salt-split routing) #

Manage salt-split assignments for a collection whose schema declares a routing field ("routing": true). One hot routing value — the mega tenant, the biggest org — funnels every write into a single partition; salting splits that value across a SET of partitions so the hot key stops being a placement bottleneck.

The API never moves data by itself: assignments state intent, the write path consumes them live (the very next write of an assigned value lands inside its partition set), and migrating documents that are already placed is a separate rehash operation. The joins tutorial walks the complete sequence against a live node.
